title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models
explain_beginner: AI language models can struggle with problems that need several reasoning steps. Earlier methods either gave hand-written examples or simply told the model to think step by step. The paper says simple step-by-step prompting often makes three mistakes: wrong arithmetic, skipped steps, and misreading the question. The authors propose Plan-and-Solve prompting. It first asks the model to plan by breaking the task into smaller parts, then asks it to complete those parts. A version called PS+ adds more detailed instructions. On ten datasets and three reasoning problems with GPT-3, this approach beat the simple step-by-step method and was competitive with other methods. It matters because it improves reasoning without examples.
explain_business: This paper suggests a prompting choice for companies using AI language models on tasks that require reasoning steps. Instead of relying on hand-written examples or an instruction to think step by step, teams can ask the model to first plan how to break the problem into smaller parts, then carry out those parts. Adding detailed instructions, called PS+, can reduce arithmetic mistakes and improve reasoning quality. In tests on ten datasets and three reasoning problems with GPT-3, this zero-shot method beat the step-by-step baseline, was comparable to or better than Zero-shot-Program-of-Thought, and was comparable to 8-shot CoT on math. It informs decisions about which prompting strategy to deploy for applications.
explain_practitioner: The authors target zero-shot multi-step reasoning, where a model is prompted without hand-crafted demonstrations. They identify three failure modes in Zero-shot-CoT: arithmetic mistakes, omitted steps, and misinterpretation of meaning. Their Plan-and-Solve method first has the model create a plan that splits the task into smaller subtasks, then execute those subtasks. PS+ adds more detailed instructions to reduce arithmetic mistakes and improve the generated reasoning steps. They tested on ten datasets covering three reasoning problems using GPT-3. The zero-shot approach consistently outperformed Zero-shot-CoT across all datasets by a large margin, was comparable to or better than Zero-shot-Program-of-Thought, and was comparable to 8-shot CoT on math reasoning.
